title: Yunus, again
hookLine: he would have stayed in the whale till the Day, had he not glorified Allah (37:143–144)

lines: WHAT IF HE NEVER CAME OUT?
cards: What if Yunus had never come out of the fish? Surah As-Saffat has a sentence about exactly that. It tells his story again, briefly: the prophet who left in anger, the ship, the lots, the great fish.
This path met him back in year one, with the three darknesses and the prayer he cried out from inside. But As-Saffat slips in a sentence found only here. An if.
If one thing about Yunus had been different, the story wouldn't have ended on a beach under a gourd vine. It wouldn't have ended at all.

teach.b: As-Saffat gives the story in ten verses. Yunus was one of the messengers. He fled to the laden ship.
Lots were drawn, and he lost. The fish swallowed him, and he was blameworthy. Then verses one forty-three and forty-four.
Pickthall: "And had he not been one of those who glorify (Allah) He would have tarried in its belly till the day when they are raised". That's the if.
The Arabic is mina'l-musabbihin, one of those who glorify, from the same root as subhanallah. Commentators read this two ways, and both are worth keeping.
Some say it means his glorifying inside the fish, the cry from year one: there's no god but You, glory to You, I was one of the wrongdoers.

teach.h: IN THE FISH, OR LONG BEFORE IT?
teach.b: Others, reported from early commentators, say it means the glorifying he'd done for years before the fish: prayer and remembrance in easy times, remembered for him in the hard one. A hadith sounds the same note.
The Prophet ﷺ told the young Ibn 'Abbas: know Allah in times of ease, and He will know you in times of hardship. On that second reading, the if isn't only about the right words at the worst moment.
It's about years of glorifying that came before the dark.
The week ran on the same thread: the man from the city's edge ran without waiting, the sun and moon keep a measure set long before, and the rows close up because people have practiced lining up.

how: Many Muslims recite the prayer of Yunus (la ilaha illa anta subhanaka inni kuntu mina z-zalimin) in times of distress, and make tasbih (subhanallah) part of daily remembrance after each prayer.

o: the prophet who was thrown into a dry well
the prophet who built an ark before the flood
the prophet in the fish, one of those who glorify

games.q: Yunus in As-Saffat — tap the pairs.
p: know Allah in times of ease

s: As-Saffat says Yunus would have stayed in the fish until the Day of Rising
had he not been one who glorifies Allah, verses 143–144.
all commentators agree the glorifying was only inside the fish
some say inside it; others say the glorifying he'd done for years before.
the root of musabbihin is the same as subhanallah
s-b-h: glorifying, declaring Allah beyond all fault.

games.q: you're Yunus, in the dark inside the fish. As-Saffat says one thing about you made the difference. what was it?
o: you were one of those who glorify Allah.
you had been right about your people.
games.why: he was one of those who glorify. commentators debate whether it means inside the fish or the years before; many keep both.

practice: Bring to mind a small tight spot from this week, a deadline, an argument, a worry, and feel where it sits in your body.
If you're Muslim, or want to try, say subhanallah, glory be to Allah, quietly, a few times while you hold it; if not, simply name the tight spot and breathe slowly beside it.
Starting while things are calm is the point, so the habit is there later.

wordCard.voice: Yunus. The prophet in the fish, who, As-Saffat says, would have stayed there until the Day of Rising if he hadn't been one who glorifies Allah. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: of those who glorify, the root of subhanallah.

carryVoice: Your line: glorifying got him out. In ease first, then in the dark. Another week, done.
